arguments.prose:
People had already gathered inside the study when I arrived: a knot of uniforms and two others who would not leave the picture. Henry stood in the doorway with his shoulders tight as if someone had wound him up and left him running; Marta hovered near the desk, hands folded, protective in the way domestic muscle learns to be. Derek, from next door, lingered in the hall—an odd presence, a man used to measuring things—and Inspector Rao kept to the edge of the room with his notebook open and his face deliberately neutral.

The study itself was obediently quiet. The heavy oak door's deadbolt had been slid from the inside. The sash window was latched; the sill bore faint gardener's pollen. Light pooled on the worn rug and threw the book spines into a dull, anonymous order. Evelyn lay where she had fallen, half-turned toward the fireplace; her fingers were clenched around a small, stubborn thing.

Her hand still clutched an engraved pocket watch; its hands had stopped at 9:07, and the case bore a hairline puncture and a faint film of oil. Beside the blotter a small folded scrap of paper was clenched in her fingers, sealed with a trace of red sealing-wax. On the desk a crystal ashtray held three cigarette butts of an uncommon coarse brand not usually smoked in the house. Near the mantel I found a small flake of red sealing-wax.

There was the smell of machine oil about the hearth—sharp and metallic in the air, like something wound too tightly and then let go. I made a point of breathing around it; smells have a way of telling the order of events better than people do.

Those are the hard things you notice and then have to explain: how a room is closed, what was in someone's hand, what the clock on a body says. But there were softer, equally important gaps: I had not seen any precise wording of Henry Crane's statement to the press. There was no record I could find of how long Marta Reyes had worked here. I couldn't tell from the material in my hands whether Rao and I had ever met before. The scrap bore a two-line cipher; I had not been given a transcription of its exact letters. What I lacked was a close, micro-description of the study's carpets and mantel—those small details the inventory summary overlooks.

Those gaps matter because motive is a ledger kept in the negative spaces as often as the positive ones. Henry's grief read public and brittle; he sat like a man holding a shape he was trying to make fit. Marta's protectiveness showed in the way she interrupted anyone who moved toward the desk, her voice low and immediate. Derek's presence was odd; he kept to the doorway as if waiting for permission to be useful.

Inspector Rao and I traded the necessary courtesies and left the room in each other's hands—his in the legal sense, mine more practical. The study would be sealed again and logged; evidence would be photographed and catalogued. For now, the scene had done its work: it had given me a lock slid from the inside, a latched window, a stopped watch with a tiny wound, wax on paper and fireplace, a crystal ashtray with three out-of-place butts, and the smell of machines in the hearth. It had also left me with questions I could not yet answer.

That, in the end, is what a locked room asks of you: not simply the obvious impossibility but the list of things you do not yet know. I pencilled them into my notebook and closed it on the study's edge; someone else would run the photographs, but I was the one who had to begin the ledger.

What I lacked was a close, micro-description of the study's carpets and mantel—those small details the inventory summary overlooks.

Those absences matter. Henry's grief read public and sharp; he held himself with the taut courtesy of someone who thinks performance protects feeling. Marta moved around the desk as if its surface were hers to defend: a hand on a corner of the blotter, a look that dared anyone to reach for the watch. Derek's presence was a different note—he lingered like a neighbour who knows the machinery of houses and notices when a machine smells wrong.

Rao and I exchanged the professional gestures required of men who are to be expected to work together: a nod, a brief mention that evidence would be photographed and the scene logged. The study would be sealed again. For now, there was only the list: a deadbolt slid from the inside; a latched sash window; a stopped watch beneath a dead woman's hand reading 9:07 with a puncture and oil on its case; wax on the note and a flake by the mantel; a crystal ashtray with three out-of-place cigarette butts; the smell of machine oil at the hearth. And the gaps—the things I could not yet put in my ledger.

I made notes. Photographing and cataloguing are someone else's ordinance; deduction is mine. A locked room is a contract that begins with a set of physical sentences and leaves you to supply the connecting verbs. I closed my notebook on that edge and let the room keep its silence a little longer—waiting is part of listening.

The heavy oak door's deadbolt had been slid from the inside. The sash window was latched; the sill showed a faint dusting of garden pollen. Light lay across the floorboards in a flat, indifferent pool. Evelyn lay where she had fallen, half-turned toward the fireplace; her fingers were clenched around a small, stubborn thing.

Her hand still clutched an engraved pocket watch; its hands had stopped at 9:07, and the case bore a hairline puncture and a faint film of oil. A small folded scrap of paper was clenched in her fingers, sealed with a trace of red sealing-wax. On the desk a crystal ashtray held three short, rough-ended butts of a coarse tobacco I did not recognise from the household's usual brand. Near the mantel I found a small flake of red sealing-wax.

There was the smell of machine oil about the hearth—sharp and metallic in the air, like a lathe left running and then abandoned. It sat in the room as insistently as any witness.

Those are the things the room offers first: how it was closed, what was in a body's hold, what time a stopped instrument insists upon. But there were other absences I noticed at once. I had not seen any precise wording of Henry Crane's statement to the press. There was no record I could find of how long Marta Reyes had worked here. I couldn't tell from the material in my hands whether Rao and I had ever met before. The scrap bore a two-line cipher; I had not been given a transcription of its exact letters. What I lacked was a close, micro-description of the study's carpets and mantel—those small details the inventory summary overlooks.

Those absences matter. Henry's grief read public and sharp; he held himself with the taut courtesy of someone who thinks performance protects feeling. Marta moved around the desk as if its surface were hers to defend: a hand on a corner of the blotter, a look that dared anyone to reach for the watch. Derek's presence was a different note—he lingered like a neighbour who knows the machinery of houses and notices when a machine smells wrong.

Rao and I exchanged the professional gestures required of men who are to be expected to work together: a nod, a brief mention that evidence would be photographed and the scene logged. The study would be sealed again. For now, there was only the list: a deadbolt slid from the inside; a latched sash window; a stopped watch beneath a dead woman's hand reading 9:07 with a puncture and oil on its case; wax on the note and a flake by the mantel; a crystal ashtray with three out-of-place cigarette butts; the smell of machine oil at the hearth. And the gaps—the things I could not yet put in my ledger.

I started where the smell was strongest and worked outwards. Inspector Rao and I lifted the hearth's low strip together; it came up with a dry complaint. Behind it was a narrow cavity, the sort of pocket a house keeps for its small embarrassments. Inside, coiled on old soot, lay a small clockwork mechanism — brass plates, a wound mainspring and a cam-mounted push-rod — its parts stained dark where oil had collected.

"Bag it and photograph it," I told Rao. "And mark the cavity." He nodded and barked the instruction down the line. The room, which had seemed merely full before, rearranged itself into evidence.

I turned the mechanism in my gloved fingers. Its brass plates were stained with the same dark oil that had smeared the watch's case. One plate bore a tiny filing nick — a maker's tic I recognised from Derek Lyle's bench. Recognition is not proof, only a direction; it made Derek's silence feel less neutral.

We took the garden together after the technical work. A lightweight aluminium extension ladder leaned against the boundary wall; one rung had a fresh scrape that matched the tell of having been used to reach the coal-hatch. The external coal chute hatch's bolt showed recent abrasion and there was coal dust in the latch groove.

I asked questions in the kitchen while Rao logged the device and the hatch. Henry told me he had been in the morning room at roughly nine. Marta said she had been serving breakfast. Derek insisted he had been in his shed. Those accounts line up politely enough on paper; the thing about alibis is that their politeness hides friction.

There were motives in the room like quiet ledgers: thin things you could read if you knew the balance. Someone mentioned Evelyn's ledger; no one put a page in front of me. I had not seen entries showing debts or payments. There was a rumour, passed with lowered voices, of a recent angry conversation — who had argued, where it had been, and what was said were all details I did not have.

The oil smelled of industry in a house that pretended not to need it. It sat at the hearth and on the device like a fingerprint. I noticed how the oil had crept into the creases of the mechanism and into the watch's punctured case; that shared stain suggested a mechanical kinship rather than a coincidence.

Rao was precise in his paperwork; he would write where the device had been found. What I did not find in the notebook on the table was a forensic phrasing of the oil staining that told me whether it smeared the hearth's lead, the mortar, or the joining timbers — a small absence that can matter later. I made a note of that omission beside the entry that promised to be the most read.

Marta watched us with a steadiness I have learned to respect; she guarded surfaces the way some people guard memories. Henry's hands were tight in his pockets; Derek's sleeves carried the faint grit of a workbench. The ladder outside and the scuffed bolt on the coal-hatch were, for the moment, the most neutral things in the case: physical traces that could be weighed without story.

When Rao stepped away to speak with a sergeant, I closed my notebook and put the device's identity under a simple instruction. I would want to examine the watch more closely, and I would want to see Derek's bench if permission could be arranged. For now, the immediate work was plain: secure the clockwork, photograph the hatch and ladder, and get me a copy of whatever ledger Evelyn kept. Those were the verbs the room had left me; they were specific enough to start with.

I took the clockwork back to the table and set it on a sheet of paper. You learn more from turning something over in your hands than from watching it sit under glass. It was small and primed to be small: a wound spring that smelled faintly of oil, a cam with a single long throw and a push-rod that looked as if it had been made to travel only a few inches.

I wound the spring a little more and let it run by hand. The cam moved with an economy that suggested a deliberate, single action rather than a continuous one; the push-rod snapped out once in a blunt, decisive motion. I timed it in my head the only way we can in a house without a laboratory: by feel. The mechanism wanted itself into a single event, and judging by the spring's resistance and the cam's pitch it would deliver that event after a short run — the sort of interval you set when you mean to catch a moment, not to keep a patrol.

That was the first thing: the clockwork was a one-shot. The second was the anatomical fact of the watch. I set Evelyn's pocket watch under a lamp and turned it slowly. The hairline puncture was at a flank, neat enough to be made by a narrow push — not a hammer, not a fall. Oil had seeped into the nick and stained the edge of the dial plate. If you want a plain sentence for an insurance company: the watch had a puncture and oil in its seam. If you want a useful sentence for an investigation: the puncture and the oil sat where a driven rod, delivered with a short, hard thrust, would meet metal.

I spread the scrap of paper on the blotter and stared at the two lines until the cipher loosened its shape. I had not promised myself a full translation; I was looking for shape. The layout was the thing: columnar marks, a repeated small loop that read like a tally, and a series of numerals or near-numerals at regular intervals. It was not a letter of complaint or a shopping list. It was a timetable — a schedule pared down to shorthand. I could not, in good faith, recite its letters here; the full transcription belonged to the promise already filed. What I could say, without inventing a line the index did not contain, was that the scrap set actions into ordered slots around the hour the watch showed.

Those three points — the clockwork's single violent throw, the watch's puncture and oil, the scrap's schedule — began to sit together like parts of a mechanism. If the push-rod could be made to emerge through the floor, a device hidden under the hearth could be set to deliver a single, timed thrust. The coal cellar lay under the study; the hatch in the garden and the ladder's scrape made the cellar accessible without drawing the front door into the business of late arrivals.

I voiced the chain out loud; to speak the hypothesis is to see how it bends. "So someone winds and sets this under the hearth, times it, and the rod reaches up through the floor at the appointed moment. The watch stops at the impact." Inspector Rao listened like a man counting evidence.

The timing was the knife-edge. The watch had stopped at 9:07; that fixed a moment you couldn't fit a long ritual around. The clockwork's wound state and its cam throw suggested a short delay between winding and action — a delay you could produce by winding, placing, and then stepping away inside the span of a few minutes. That meant the act of placement and the act of being at a bench were not mutually compatible if both required presence at the same minute.

Derek's claim that he had been in his shed filing brass all morning looked less neat when you applied the clockwork's calendar. He had the skill the maker's nick suggested and the means to make a device like this. He also had the ladder opportunity implied by the scuff on the rung and the hatch abrasion. If the device had to be wound and positioned so close to nine, someone with both the bench and the garden route had the easiest access. Derek's alibi shifted from plausible to fragile.

Rao asked the practical question next—photographs, measurements, a warrant to see the shed—things that make hypotheses accountable. I wrote the items down: more photographs of the puncture; controlled unwinding of the clockwork in a lab; a look at Derek's bench. For the moment, the story narrowed: the watch stopped at 9:07; the device was built for a single thrust; the scrap was a schedule. There was a plausible line from bench to hatch to hearth to watch. Whether the line led to Derek or to coincidence was a thing you proved with work. I put that not as accusation but as the next thing to prove.
